chapterBreakdown.gentle:

Morning, late afternoon, tired evening, it should not matter. Keller says that confidence is misplaced. Willpower is not always on call. Important effort is real, but it is not available with equal strength in every window of the day.

That matters because people often build plans as if timing does not exist. They push the hardest writing, studying, or decision-making into whatever space is left after reactive work, messages, errands, and fatigue have already taken their share. Then they expect heroic effort to rescue the task later. The chapter says that strategy quietly weakens the result before the work even starts.

The chapter's mechanism is placement. A person may still have enough energy for small tasks after a draining day, but that does not mean the same quality of judgment is available for the task that most needs depth. Hard effort placed in a weak window pays a bad timing tax. It becomes slower, thinner, and more dependent on trying to manufacture force that would have arrived more naturally in a fresher slot.

He is saying that serious work should not be scheduled as if all moments are equal. Respecting timing is a form of discipline because it protects the task instead of asking it to survive unnecessary disadvantage.

The chapter becomes practical immediately. In work, it means guarding the freshest block for the hard judgment that actually changes the project. In school, it means not always saving the most demanding material for the most depleted hour. In personal life, it means bringing meaningful decisions into a clearer window before fatigue and scattered obligations distort them. Keller says that assumption is false. Willpower matters, but it is not uniformly available across the day, and important work gets distorted when that reality is ignored.

The chapter matters because bad timing is one of the easiest ways to weaken meaningful effort while still looking responsible. A person handles reactive tasks all day, pushes the important work into the remaining slot, and then expects discipline to carry it across the line. The plan feels respectable because the task still appears on the calendar. But the chapter says the real problem started earlier, when the task was placed in a weak window.

This is the chapter's central mechanism. Not every hour carries the same quality of attention, judgment, or cognitive freshness. A draining day can leave enough energy for maintenance work without leaving enough for high-value thinking. When that difference is ignored, the important task pays a bad timing tax. The person has to rebuild force that would have been more available in a fresher slot. The work may still get done, but it often gets done thinner.

That is also why the chapter should stay cleaner than pop-psychology theater. The point does not depend on fake depletion statistics or borrowed biology language. The ordinary experience is enough.
